title: Feathers of the Roseate Spoonbill
bodyHtml:
Classical Nahuatl was the language of the Aztec Empire. Although Classical Nahuatl is no longer actively spoken, it is related to modern Nahuatl, which has approximately 1.5 million speakers, mainly in Mexico.

Over the centuries, scholars have proposed several different writing systems for representing Classical Nahuatl. Some early approaches from the 16th century were based on the system used for Spanish at the time. However, this approach faced challenges in how to represent sounds and distinctions that were not present in Spanish.

One solution is to use the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA). The IPA is designed to represent all sounds of human speech unambiguously, and so it provides a reliable transcription system that can be read by linguists across the world. However, the IPA is often unwieldy and does not reflect the needs of particular language communities. Therefore, the IPA is rarely used by non-linguists.

Some more recent proposals are therefore designed specifically with Nahuatl in mind, in order to ensure both ease of use (which the IPA lacks) and faithfulness to the language (which the 16th-century systems lacked). To illustrate some of the writing systems that have been proposed over the years, the name of the Nahuatl language can be written as nahuatlatolli in a 16th-century writing system, /nawatɬaʔtoːlli/ in the IPA, or nahuatlàtōlli in a 20th-century writing system.

Below is the first stanza of a Nahuatl poem, “The Song of Temilotzin.” On the left is the poem as it appears in a manuscript of the 16th century (modified slightly for clarity). On the right, the text has been rewritten in a system proposed more recently, in the 20th century.

16th-century writing system20th-century writing system
Ye nihualla, antocnihuan in:Ye nihuāllâ, antocnīhuān in:
noconcozcazoya,noconcōzcazōya,
nictzinitzcamana,nictzinitzcamana,
nictlauhquecholihuimolohua,nictlāuhquechōlihuimolohua,
nicteocuitlaicuiya,nicteōcuitlaìcuiya,
nicquetzalhuixtoilpiznicquetzalhuixtoilpīz
in icniuhyotl.in icnīuhyōtl.
Niccuicailacatzoa cohuayotl.Niccuīcailacatzoa cōhuayōtl.
In teucpan nicquixtiz,In tēucpan nicquīxtīz,
an ya tonmochin,ān ya tonmochīn,
quin icuac tonmochin in otiyaquequin ìcuāc tonmochīn in ōtiyàquê
    ye Mictlan.    ye Mictlān.
In iuh ca zan tictlanehuico.In iuh ca zan tictlānehuīcô.

Here are some words and phrases from “The Song of Temilotzin” in the 16th-century writing system, along with their equivalents in the IPA, as well as English translations:

16th-centuryIPAEnglish
nictlauhquecholihuimolohua/niktɬaːwketʃoːliwimolowa/‘I adorn it with feathers of the roseate spoonbill (a kind of bird)’
nicteocuitlaicuiya/nikteoːkʷitɬaiʔkʷija/‘I wrap it with coils of gold’
nicquetzalhuixtoilpiz in icniuhyotl/nikketsalwiʃtoilpiːs in ikniːwjoːtɬ/‘I have bound up our friendship like a captive with feathers of the quetzal (another kind of bird)’
in teucpan nicquixtiz/in teːkʷpan nikkiːʃtiːs/‘I will make it emerge in the palace’
otiyaque ye Mictlan/oːtijaʔkeʔ je miktɬaːn/‘we will have gone to Mictlan (the land of the dead)’

questions.partPrompt: Convert the following phrases from the 16th-century writing system into the IPA.
Convert the following words from the IPA into the 20th-century writing system.

In set theory (a branch of mathematics), it is said that there is a bijection between two sets if it is possible to convert from one set to the other and back without losing any information. This concept can be extended to describe writing systems. For example, there is a bijection between the set of numbers written in numerals (e.g., 43 or 11) and the set of numbers written in letters (e.g., forty-three or eleven). If you ignore capitalization, there is a bijection between two of the writing systems discussed here.
questions.answerKey: the 20th-century writing system and the IPA

the IPA and the 20th-century writing system

hints.text: Line up the same word in all three systems. The two spellings of the poem differ only in extra marks (macrons like ā, and the accents à and â), so those marks must stand for something the IPA also shows.

Two things are audible in the IPA but simply missing from the 16th-century spelling: vowel length (marked with ː) and the glottal stop ʔ (the catch in the middle of English uh-oh). The 20th-century system writes length with a macron over the vowel and a glottal stop with a grave accent on the vowel before it inside a word, or a circumflex at the end of a word. Everything else is a straight letter-for-sound match, though a few sounds have two spellings depending on what follows: k is c before a, o, a consonant or word-end but qu before i and e; kʷ is cu before a vowel but uc before a consonant or word-end; w is hu before a vowel but uh otherwise.

Work through a line that is not asked about. The 16th-century line in teucpan nicquixtiz corresponds to IPA /in teːkʷpan nikkiːʃtiːs/: the uc in teucpan is kʷ before a consonant, qu in nicquixtiz is just k before i, x is ʃ, and the final z is s. Now add the length marks the IPA shows and you get the 20th-century In tēucpan nicquīxtīz. Try the reverse direction on that same line to check your rules.

explanationHtml:
What the problem is really about

You are given the same Nahuatl poem in two spelling systems, plus a handful of words in the IPA (the International Phonetic Alphabet, where each symbol stands for exactly one sound). The job is to work out how the three systems line up, letter by letter and sound by sound.

Two IPA symbols matter a lot here:

  • ː after a vowel means the vowel is long (held longer). Nahuatl uses length to tell words apart, so it is real information.
  • ʔ is a glottal stop, the little catch in the throat in the middle of English “uh-oh.”

Step 1: compare the two spellings of the poem

Look at line 1: 16th-century Ye nihualla, antocnihuan in: versus 20th-century Ye nihuāllâ, antocnīhuān in:. The letters are identical; only marks have been added. So the 20th-century system is the 16th-century system plus extra marks.

Which marks? A macron (ā, ē, ī, ō), a grave accent (à, ì), and a circumflex (â, ê, ô).

Step 2: match those marks to the IPA

Take nicteocuitlaicuiya = /nikteoːkʷitɬaiʔkʷija/, written nicteōcuitlaìcuiya in the 20th century.

  • Where the IPA has oː, the 20th-century text has ō. So macron = long vowel.
  • Where the IPA has aiʔ, the 20th-century text has aì. So grave accent on a vowel = a glottal stop right after it, when it is inside the word.

Now check the end of a word: otiyaque = /oːtijaʔkeʔ/ = ōtiyàquê. The word-internal aʔ is à, and the final eʔ is ê. So circumflex = glottal stop at the end of a word.

Step 3: the plain letter-to-sound rules

Both spellings borrow habits from 16th-century Spanish:

SpellingIPAWhere
ckbefore a, o, a consonant, or word-end
qukbefore i, e
cukʷbefore a vowel
uckʷbefore a consonant or word-end
csbefore i, e
zsbefore a, o, a consonant, or word-end
tztseverywhere
tltɬeverywhere
chtʃeverywhere
xʃeverywhere
yjeverywhere
huwbefore a vowel
uhwbefore a consonant or word-end

Notice the neat pattern: the “w-ish” sounds kʷ and w are written with the u on the left of the consonant letter when nothing follows, and on the right when a vowel follows.

Step 4: G1, spelling into IPA

Here the 20th-century poem is your friend, because it tells you where the long vowels and glottal stops are.

  • ye nihualla appears as Ye nihuāllâ. So: y = j, e = e, ni = ni, hu before a vowel = w, ā = aː, ll = ll (a long l, not the Spanish “ly” sound), â = a plus glottal stop. Result: /je niwaːllaʔ/.
  • antocnihuan in appears as antocnīhuān in. The c before n is k; ī = iː; hu = w; ā = aː. Result: /antokniːwaːn in/.
  • quin icuac appears as quin ìcuāc. qu before i = k; ì = i plus glottal stop; cu before a vowel = kʷ; ā = aː; final c = k. Result: /kin iʔkʷaːk/.

Step 5: G2, IPA into the 20th-century system

  • /weːweʔ/: w before a vowel is hu, so we get hu + ē + hu + e; the final glottal stop turns that last e into ê. Answer: huēhuê.
  • /tʃokolaːtɬ/: tʃ = ch, aː = ā, tɬ = tl. Answer: chocolātl.
  • /miktɬaːnteːkʷtɬi/: k before a consonant = c, tɬ = tl, aː = ā, eː = ē, and kʷ before a consonant = uc. Answer: Mictlāntēuctli (the same tēuc- you can see in tēucpan ‘palace’, literally ‘lord-place’).

Step 6: G3, the bijection

A bijection means you can convert in either direction and get back exactly what you started with. The 16th-century system throws away information: it never marks vowel length or glottal stops, so nihualla could in principle be read several ways, and you cannot recover nihuāllâ from it without knowing the language. That rules out any pairing involving the 16th-century system.

The 20th-century system and the IPA, however, encode exactly the same information. Every 20th-century letter or letter pair maps to one IPA symbol, and the choices between c/qu, cu/uc and hu/uh are fully predictable from the surrounding letters, so the mapping runs cleanly both ways. The bijection is between the 20th-century writing system and the IPA.
